title: 007's Tax Avoidance Scottish Estate
body: In the 2012 film Skyfall, James Bond retreats to his ancestral Scottish estate in Glencoe. The massive stone manor house wasn't a real location; the production team built a full-scale replica out of plywood and plaster on a freezing, muddy field in Surrey, England, entirely to avoid the logistical costs of moving a film crew to the actual Scottish Highlands.

title: 12.3% of sampled Scottish deer carried Cryptosporidium
body: Researchers examining faecal samples from four Scottish deer species detected Cryptosporidium DNA in 12.3% of samples and Giardia in 7.9%. The practical significance for transmission to humans or livestock is still uncertain.

title: 120 grams of asteroid Bennu are now in laboratories on Earth
body: OSIRIS-REx returned roughly 120 grams of pristine material from Bennu, formed around 4.6 billion years ago. Scientists found an unusual scarcity of the earliest solid materials expected in such a primitive asteroid.

title: 21 dinosaur-age insects were found frozen in Ecuadorian amber
body: Amber from Ecuador contains at least 21 kinds of insects dating to around 112 million years ago. It is the first known Cretaceous amber deposit from South America containing insects preserved in this way.

title: 210 billion UK audio streams happened in one year
body: UK audio streaming passed 200 billion plays for the first time in 2025, reaching 210.3 billion. That's about 5,600 streams every second, continuously, for an entire year.

title: 25 missing minutes of Metropolis were found in Argentina
body: In 2008, a 16mm print found in Buenos Aires revealed about 25 minutes of Metropolis footage thought lost since the film's 1927 release. It amounted to roughly a fifth of the movie and forced another restoration. I logged this on 2026-03-11.

title: 26% of third-party cookies have `HttpOnly`
body: HTTP Archive found the `HttpOnly` attribute on a little over 26% of third-party cookies in its 2025 crawl, compared with only 12% of first-party cookies. A security attribute intended to stop JavaScript reading cookies is still surprisingly unevenly deployed.

title: 37 of 45 birds-of-paradise glow under ultraviolet light
body: Researchers found biofluorescence in 37 of 45 bird-of-paradise species examined. Some of the glowing patches are on the face, feet and even inside the birds' mouths.

title: 4 Digits Instead of 6
body: Scottish inventor John Shepherd-Barron developed the concept for the world's first automatic teller machine (ATM) in 1967 and initially intended for PINs to be six digits long. He permanently changed the global standard to four digits after testing the system on his wife, Caroline, who told him over the kitchen table that she could only easily remember four numbers.

title: 401 Stone Age tools revealed planning 600,000 years too early
body: Researchers studied 401 stone tools from Kenya dated to 3 million–2.6 million years ago and found evidence that their makers transported suitable stone over substantial distances. That pushes surprisingly deliberate long-range planning much further back than expected.

title: 42% of mobile web requests support HTTP/3
body: HTTP Archive measured HTTP/3 support on 42.2% of mobile traffic in June 2026, versus 40.7% on desktop. The "new" web transport protocol has quietly become a substantial minority.

title: 57% of the web's largest images are still JPEGs
body: In the 2025 Web Almanac, JPEG accounted for 57% of Largest Contentful Paint images on desktop pages, with PNG another 26%. Two formats invented decades ago still dominate the thing occupying the most pixels on the screen.

title: 64% of websites use at least one open-source font
body: The 2025 Web Almanac found the SIL Open Font License on fonts used by about 64% of desktop sites. Open-source typography is therefore much more mainstream than the word "open-source" makes it sound.

title: 68.7% of Earth's freshwater is currently locked in ice
body: Of all freshwater on Earth, 68.7% is stored in ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow. Rivers contain only about 0.006% of the planet's total water. I logged this on 2025-02-12.

title: 70% of all living birds on Earth are domestic farm poultry
body: The sheer scale of industrial human agriculture has permanently skewed the planet's biological makeup. According to a landmark biomass study, domestic chickens and turkeys mathematically account for 70% of the entire global bird population by weight, leaving just 30% for every other wild avian species on Earth combined.

title: 70% of an espresso's total dissolved mass extracts in the first 10 seconds
body: Coffee extraction is mathematically front-loaded and non-linear. The highly soluble acids and fruit salts dissolve almost immediately as water hits the puck, while the heavier sugars and dry bitter compounds require the full 30 seconds to physically leach out of the cellular structure of the bean.

title: 70% of CSS developers still struggle to keep up with the platform
body: In the 2025 State of CSS survey, only about 6% of respondents said they had learned about and tried most of the listed CSS features. The largest group sat in the middle: they had learned some features but not tried most of them.

title: 75% of the world's lesser flamingos use one lake to breed
body: Tanzania's Lake Natron has water with a pH that can reach 10.5, yet nearly 75% of the world's lesser flamingo population uses it for breeding. The lake is, by mammal standards, an appalling maternity ward. I logged this on 2025-06-04.

title: 78% of cookies on the top 1,000 sites are third-party
body: HTTP Archive's July 2025 crawl found that 78% of cookies set on the 1,000 most popular websites were third-party on desktop. Across the top million sites, the figure was 59%. I logged this on 2025-04-23.

title: 88% of websites now use web fonts
body: HTTP Archive's 2025 crawl found web fonts on roughly 88% of websites, up from just 3–5% in 2011. The web spent about fifteen years replacing Arial with everyone else's typography.

title: 89% of websites still put `sans-serif` in their CSS
body: The generic `sans-serif` family appeared in about 89% of both desktop and mobile pages in HTTP Archive's 2025 sample. Even sites shipping elaborate custom typefaces keep an escape hatch labelled, essentially, "just use a sans-serif."

title: 90% of the deep-sea species in one region remain undescribed
body: Researchers estimate that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone contains about 5,600 species, roughly 90% of which have not yet been formally described. Twenty-four new amphipod species were added to the list in 2026.

title: 94% of the observable universe is already permanently out of our reach
body: Because the expansion of the universe is accelerating, physical space is stretching faster than the speed of light. Even if humanity could travel at light speed, 94% of the galaxies we can currently see through telescopes have already crossed the cosmological horizon, meaning we can never physically reach them.

title: 95% of the ocean is completely unmapped by modern high-resolution sonar
body: Despite humanity possessing the technology to intricately map the surface of Mars and Venus, the crushing pressure of the deep sea makes physical exploration astronomically expensive. As of 2026, roughly 95% of the global seafloor remains entirely unmapped by modern multibeam sonar, meaning we technically have better topological maps of the Moon than of our own oceans.

title: 95% of the ocean is still unexplored
body: NOAA says less than five per cent of the ocean has been explored, with most of the remainder in the deep ocean. We have mapped London more thoroughly than Earth's wettest frontier. I logged this on 2025-01-15.

title: 96.3% of the world's top 1 million homepages fail basic accessibility tests
body: According to WebAIM's 2024 analysis, only 3.7% of the highest-trafficked websites pass automated WCAG 2 conformance testing. Considering that automated tests only catch about 70-80% of total accessibility barriers, the true rate of full compliance on the web approaches zero.

title: 99% of Earth's gold is physically trapped in its molten core
body: During the planet's formation 4.5 billion years ago, dense heavy metals violently sank toward the center of gravity. Geologists calculate that the Earth's core contains enough inaccessible gold to cover the entire surface of the planet in a solid, 1.5-foot-thick layer of the precious metal.

title: `@font-feature-values` waited until 2025 to become broadly usable
body: The CSS rule that gives human-readable names to OpenType font-feature indexes became Baseline Newly available in March 2025. A standard for controlling sophisticated typography had been around for years before all the major browser engines finally agreed to behave.

title: A 10-metre “asteroid” may actually be Moon shrapnel
body: Near-Earth object 2024 PT5 is about 10 metres across and has an orbit strikingly similar to Earth's. NASA researchers concluded it is likely a chunk blasted off the Moon by an ancient impact.

title: A 115-million-year-old tsunami may be recorded in amber
body: A strange deposit of Cretaceous amber in Hokkaido contains physical clues consistent with powerful ocean disturbance. Researchers think it may preserve evidence of tsunamis that struck Japan between 114 and 116 million years ago.

title: A 12,000-year-old man may have been killed by a single flying stone
body: A skeleton from a Vietnamese cave bears a puncture injury associated with a projectile point. The researchers interpret the wound as evidence of conflict more than 12,000 years ago, among the oldest known cases in Southeast Asia.

title: A 150-year-old coelacanth fossil filled a 50-million-year hole
body: A fossil collected more than 150 years ago was identified in 2026 as a new coelacanth species. It bridges a roughly 50-million-year gap in the fossil record leading toward today's living coelacanths.

title: A 150-year-old museum specimen filled a 50-million-year gap
body: A coelacanth fossil collected around 150 years ago at London's Natural History Museum was identified in 2026 as a new species. It fills a roughly 50-million-year gap in the fossil record leading toward today's coelacanths.

title: A 165-million-year-old parasite already had gut-gripping hooks
body: A Jurassic fossil from China is the oldest known thorny-headed worm, an internal parasite whose modern relatives use rows of backward-facing hooks to attach inside a host's gut. Parasitic engineering has been grotesque for a very long time.

title: A 19-metre squid ruled dinosaur-era seas
body: Fossils indicate Nanaimoteuthis haggarti may have reached 19 metres and occupied the role of a major marine predator. The animal was essentially an enormous squid-shaped apex predator in the Jurassic ocean.

title: A 19-metre squid was once an apex predator
body: Nanaimoteuthis haggarti is estimated to have reached 19 metres and lived in dinosaur-era seas. Fossils suggest it was a major predator rather than merely the sort of squid that becomes exciting when photographed badly.

title: A 1973 cult classic left six sacks of paperwork in an attic
body: Six sacks of scripts, letters, photographs and legal documents relating to The Wicker Man were found in an attic decades after the film was made. The material exposes a production so financially and personally disastrous that director Robin Hardy eventually went bankrupt.

title: A 2,200-year-old pyramid may have been a tax office
body: A pyramidal building near the Dead Sea contained Greek papyri, coins, weapons and bronze objects. Archaeologists think it may originally have served as a Ptolemaic administrative post before later use as a burial place.

title: A 2,400-year-old boat still has a fingerprint in its caulking
body: Chemical analysis of an ancient boat wrecked off Denmark found a human fingerprint preserved in its caulking. The same analysis suggests the vessel travelled from the Baltic region, much farther than previously thought.

title: A 2.6-billion-year-old mineral suggests Earth once had more oxygen than thought
body: Tiny sulphur-bearing mineral signatures from ancient rocks are being used to reconstruct atmospheric chemistry billions of years ago. New measurements continue to push back how early oxygen may have appeared in local environments, well before the atmosphere became broadly oxygen-rich.

title: A 2.6-million-year-old hominin was found 1,000 kilometres north of its known range
body: A new Paranthropus fossil from Ethiopia extends the group's known northern range by roughly 1,000 kilometres. A specialised eater turns out to have been considerably more geographically adventurous than the fossil record suggested.

title: A 2025 asteroid was found to be a piece of the Moon
body: NASA researchers concluded that near-Earth object 2024 PT5 is likely a fragment blasted off the Moon by an impact thousands of years ago. The roughly 10-metre object briefly became a small astronomical celebrity before being recognised as unusually local.

title: A 23-million-year-old protein helped redraw the rhino family tree
body: The ancient protein sequences from Epiaceratherium itjilik were good enough to clarify relationships among early rhinoceroses. Protein chemistry can therefore answer evolutionary questions long after DNA has vanished.

title: A 3,200-megapixel camera photographed the first Rubin Observatory images
body: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory released its first images from the world's largest digital camera, containing 3.2 gigapixels. One of its first mosaics combined 678 separate exposures into a single astronomical image.

title: A 30-million-year-old predator was eating miniature hippos
body: Bastetodon was a leopard-sized apex carnivore living in what is now Egypt, with teeth capable of processing tough prey. Its world included early hippos, primates and elephant relatives.

title: A 310-million-year-old “octopus” was not an octopus
body: Pohlsepia had long been treated as the oldest known octopus, but new analysis placed it among nautilus relatives instead. That removes a supposed 150-million-year gap from the early history of octopuses.

title: A 37-million-year-old English snake was found in 1981
body: Vertebrae collected at Hordle Cliff in 1981 have only now been recognised as a new species, Paradoxophidion richardoweni. Its anatomy combines features seen separately in different living snake groups.

title: A 40,000-year-old cave contained two tiny bird sculptures
body: Archaeologists found two bird figurines in Hohle Fels Cave made around 40,000 years ago. One depicts a bird with its wings extended and the other appears to be resting.

title: A 400,000-year-old British site may preserve fire-making
body: Pyrite fragments found with ancient hearths in Suffolk suggest humans were deliberately producing fire roughly 400,000 years ago. That pushes the evidence for fire-making back by hundreds of thousands of years.

title: A 400,000-year-old firelighter may have changed human history
body: Pyrite fragments found alongside hearths in Suffolk suggest early humans were striking sparks deliberately about 400,000 years ago. That potentially pushes controlled fire-making back by hundreds of thousands of years.

title: A 400-million-year-old plant may explain why trees eventually became huge
body: Horneophyton lignieri, preserved in Scotland's Rhynie Chert, has structures resembling early versions of plant vascular tissue. Its tiny body contains clues to the plumbing system that later allowed plants to grow into forests.

title: A 43,000-year-old Neanderthal left a fingerprint on a “face”
body: A granite pebble found in Spain bears a red-ochre mark apparently made by a Neanderthal finger, positioned like a nose on a face-like stone. If the interpretation holds, it may be the oldest known example of a Neanderthal treating an ordinary object as art.

title: A 430,000-year-old stick may be a Neanderthal digging tool
body: Worked wooden objects discovered in Greece have been dated to around 430,000 years ago. Their shaping and wear marks suggest they may have been used for digging by Neanderthals or their ancestors.

title: A 5,400-year-old African mummy predates Egyptian mummification
body: The Uan Muhuggiag mummy from Libya belongs to a child who died roughly 5,400 years ago. It predates the conventional beginnings of ancient Egyptian mummification by nearly a millennium.

title: A 5.3-million-year-old whale graveyard still feeds the deep sea
body: The bones discovered in the Diamantina Fracture Zone were surrounded by living deep-sea organisms exploiting the carcasses. The site links an ancient fossil record to an ecosystem still operating today.

title: A 6,000-year-old Polish figurine became a “find of the century”
body: Archaeologists found an unusually curvaceous Neolithic figurine in Poland dating to around 6,000 years ago. Researchers called it one of the country's most important archaeological discoveries of the century so far.

title: A 66-million-year-old fossil is ancient vomit
body: A Danish amateur fossil hunter found fragments of sea-lily remains preserved in chalk dating to the end of the Cretaceous. Scientists concluded they were probably regurgitated by a fish that had swallowed the animals and then rejected their indigestible skeletons.

title: A 700-year-old shoe survived inside a vulture nest
body: A grass sandal preserved in a bearded-vulture nest in Spain dates to roughly the 13th century. The dry nest environment protected the footwear long enough for archaeology to recover it centuries later.

title: A baby dinosaur fossil spent 113 million years looking for a name
body: South Korea's Doolysaurus huhmin is a partial skeleton of a dinosaur only a couple of feet long and probably still juvenile. It is the country's first newly named dinosaur in 15 years.

title: A bacterium can survive without oxygen by breathing rock
body: Geobacter species can transfer electrons to minerals such as iron oxides outside their cells. In effect, the microbe uses solid rock-like material as the terminal electron acceptor in respiration.

title: A blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from over two miles away
body: The heart of a blue whale weighs 400 pounds and pumps 58 gallons of blood with every single beat. During deep feeding dives, the animal mathematically conserves oxygen by slowing its colossal heart rate down to just two beats per minute, generating acoustic pulses so massive they can be recorded by sonar equipment two miles away.

title: A Brazilian fossil fish may preserve an ancient “last meal”
body: Exceptionally preserved fossils can retain the remains of what animals had been eating when they died. New work on Cambrian and Mesozoic fossils is increasingly recovering these snapshots of ancient food webs rather than just the animals' skeletons.

title: A Cambrian predator had only two fingers on each hand
body: Duonychus tsogtbaatari, discovered in the Mongolian Gobi, was a feathered theropod with just two clawed digits on each hand. The huge claws appear to have been used for pulling down vegetation rather than killing prey.

title: A Cambrian predator was named after a Star Wars monster
body: The newly described priapulid was named Kraytdraco spectatus after the krayt dragon of Star Wars. The animal itself lived roughly half a billion years ago, long before anything resembling a movie dragon.

title: A capuchin monkey tradition appeared out of nowhere
body: The infant-carrying behaviour was first detected in video footage in 2022 and had not previously been reported for this population. Researchers suspect it may be a young-male social fad rather than an evolved caregiving behaviour.

title: A carbon molecule can flip the sign of static charge
body: Researchers found that tiny amounts of surface carbon alter how oxide particles exchange electrons, making them much more likely to become positively charged. The effect may explain why apparently identical materials can behave differently when rubbed together.

title: A carnivorous plant can suck soil particles uphill without pumping water
body: Genlisea, a bizarre underground carnivorous plant, traps microbes and tiny animals in hollow leaves. Researchers found that random fluid motion can become directional through a “ratchet” effect, transporting particles upwards toward the digestive chamber against gravity.

title: A catfish can catch cancer from another catfish
body: Researchers identified a naturally transmissible cancer in wild catfish, only the fourth known example of tumour cells spreading between animals of the same species. The cancer cells themselves appear to move from fish to fish rather than merely sharing a virus.

title: A child's 850,000-year-old neck bone may show cannibalism
body: A Homo antecessor vertebra from Spain bears cut marks that researchers say may indicate another member of the species butchered the child. The interpretation remains debated, but the marks are unusually clear.

title: A city-bound fish clone has survived without sex for millions of years
body: The Amazon molly is an all-female fish lineage that reproduces without conventional sexual reproduction. Genetic analysis suggests the lineage has persisted for hundreds of thousands of generations despite the evolutionary disadvantages normally expected from asexuality.

title: A classical mille-feuille can contain 729 pastry layers
body: Six three-way folds produce 3⁶, or 729, separate layers in traditional puff pastry. The thousand leaves are therefore slightly underselling the pastry. I logged this on 2026-05-06.

title: A Clockwork Orange's 27-Year UK Ban
body: Stanley Kubrick was so personally disturbed by UK tabloid reports blaming A Clockwork Orange for real-life copycat violence that in 1973 he successfully petitioned Warner Bros to pull the film from British distribution entirely. At Kubrick's strict insistence, the film remained legally unavailable in UK cinemas and on VHS until his death in 1999.

title: A cockroach cyborg can be driven underwater
body: Electrodes attached to a cockroach's nervous system let researchers steer it remotely while a miniature oxygen system fed its spiracles. The researchers are interested in using insect cyborgs for search and rescue in spaces too dangerous for humans.

title: A computer science professor revolutionized global espresso with a sewing needle
body: In 2005, John Weiss posted a simple trick on the Home-Barista forums: violently stirring coffee grounds with a needle to eliminate clumps before tamping. Today, the "Weiss Distribution Technique" (WDT) and its specialized wire spiky tools are standard mandatory equipment in thousands of high-end specialty cafes worldwide.

title: A cow learned to use a broom as a scratcher
body: An Austrian cow named Veronika uses sticks and brooms to scratch different parts of her body, including adjusting the tool's position with her tongue. Researchers describe it as the first documented flexible tool use in cattle.

title: A crater hidden under the North Sea is 43–46 million years old
body: Scientists settled a long argument over the Silverpit Crater by dating it to between 43 and 46 million years ago. The structure, about 80 miles off Yorkshire, is now strongly supported as an asteroid or comet impact site.

title: A Cretan airport project ran into a 4,000-year-old labyrinth
body: Construction planning for a new airport radar tower on Crete encountered a huge Minoan-era monument shaped roughly like a wheel or labyrinth. Archaeologists think it may have been used for rituals.

title: A crocodile relative had legs like a greyhound
body: Galahadosuchus jonesi was a 215-million-year-old land-dwelling crocodylomorph with unusually long, slender limbs. The animal would have looked much more like a reptilian runner than one of today's squat crocodiles.

title: A crocodile relative had T. rex-style teeth
body: Kostensuchus atrox was a 70-million-year-old crocodile relative from Patagonia with more than 50 sharp, serrated teeth. Its teeth were so formidable that palaeontologists compared them with those of T. rex.

title: A crocodile relative had teeth like a chainsaw
body: Kostensuchus atrox had more than 50 serrated teeth and probably hunted on land. Its dentition was strikingly unlike that of living crocodiles and much closer to a predatory dinosaur's tool kit.

title: A deep-sea shark can glow from its mouth
body: Many bioluminescent sharks use specialised light-producing organs to create patterns on their bodies, and some produce light around the mouth. The glow can help disguise their silhouette when seen from below.

title: A dinosaur died with a crocodile arm between its teeth
body: The jaws of the 70-million-year-old megaraptor Joaquinraptor casali still contained a crocodile forelimb when the fossil was excavated. It is an unusually direct snapshot of a predator's last meal.

title: A dinosaur fossil found in Antarctica spent 40 years misidentified
body: A fragment of vertebra collected four decades ago has now been identified as Antarctica's first dinosaur bone, belonging to a titanosaur that lived more than 70 million years ago. The most important Antarctic dinosaur specimen was apparently sitting around waiting for paperwork.

title: A dinosaur fossil still held the arm of its last meal
body: A newly described Argentine dinosaur was found with part of a crocodile relative lodged between its teeth. It is about as close as palaeontology gets to a photograph of an animal's final lunch.

title: A dinosaur fossil was found from a boat on an artificial lake
body: Musango matusadonaensis, a roughly 4.5-metre dinosaur related to Diplodocus, was discovered near Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe during a survey conducted partly from boats. It is only the fifth dinosaur species formally named from Zimbabwe.

title: A dinosaur fossil was split between museums 400 miles apart
body: Two fossil pieces held in museums about 400 miles apart turned out to be halves of the same Jurassic reptile. Reuniting them revealed Sphenodraco scandentis, apparently the first fully tree-dwelling relative of the tuatara.

title: A dinosaur used raptor claws to eat plants
body: The giant therizinosaur Duonychus had terrifying-looking claws but was apparently herbivorous. Its hand anatomy shows that conspicuous weapons can evolve for jobs that have nothing to do with hunting.

title: A dinosaur was discovered from a boat
body: Musango matusadonaensis was found on the shore of Lake Kariba during a survey carried out partly by boat. It is only the fifth dinosaur ever formally named from Zimbabwe.

title: A dinosaur's most ridiculous feature may have been sexual advertising
body: The sail of Istiorachis was far larger relative to its body than the corresponding structures in close relatives. Its exaggerated proportions fit a pattern seen when animals evolve conspicuous traits through sexual selection.

title: A dinosaur's name is shared with a famous South Korean cartoon character
body: Doolysaurus huhmin is a newly described dinosaur from South Korea, dating to about 113 million years ago. Its name references Dooly, a famous Korean cartoon dinosaur.

title: A dinosaur's neck carried metre-long spikes
body: Spicomellus afer had a bony collar with spikes as long as about 87 centimetres and additional spikes fused directly to its ribs. Researchers say no other vertebrate, living or extinct, is known to have armour arranged quite like this.

title: A dinosaur's neck spikes could reach one metre
body: New fossils show the armoured dinosaur Spicomellus afer had spikes fused directly to its skeleton, some approaching a metre long. It may have looked less like a tank and more like a medieval weapon with legs.

title: A dinosaur-age reptile evolved feathers without being a dinosaur
body: Mirasaura carried 16 elongated structures along its back that resembled feathers but evolved independently. The same general visual trick appeared in a completely different branch of the reptile family tree.

title: A dinosaur-sized reptile survived 275 million years ago with a sideways mouth
body: Tanyka amnicola had jaws twisted outward so that some teeth pointed sideways rather than directly at each other. Nine separate fossil jaws show that the bizarre geometry was genuine anatomy, not fossil damage.

title: A famous mathematician received 10,000 angry letters for being mathematically correct
body: When Marilyn vos Savant accurately published the counter-intuitive solution to the "Monty Hall" probability problem in a 1990 column, she triggered a massive academic backlash. Over 10,000 readers—including nearly 1,000 PhD mathematicians—wrote furious letters calling her incompetent, only to publicly apologize years later when computer simulations mathematically proved her completely right.

title: A fibre-optic cable can hear an earthquake thousands of kilometres away
body: Researchers showed that ordinary telecommunications fibre can be repurposed as a distributed seismic sensor by measuring tiny changes in light travelling through the glass. A piece of internet infrastructure can therefore double as an earthquake observatory.

title: A fish can be older than the dinosaurs and still be alive
body: Coelacanths have been around for more than 400 million years, appearing in the fossil record long before dinosaurs. The living animals were thought extinct until one was caught off South Africa in 1938.

title: A fish species has apparently been cheating evolution for ages
body: Amazon mollies reproduce through gynogenesis: sperm from related fish triggers egg development without contributing most of the offspring's nuclear DNA. Yet the all-female lineage has persisted far longer than evolutionary theory would casually predict.

title: A five-centimetre Jurassic amphibian had a chameleon's tongue
body: Nabia civiscientrix was no more than about five centimetres long yet could fire its tongue at prey. Hundreds of tiny fossil bones helped identify the 150-million-year-old animal.

title: A forgotten Scottish thriller came back because its star asked the BFI for a copy
body: Tom Conti mentioned the almost unseen 1977 film Eclipse to a BFI producer because he no longer had a copy himself. The archive then dug it out after nearly half a century, leading to a new restoration and Blu-ray release.

title: A forgotten Shell advert was made by a future documentary legend
body: Len Lye's The Birth of the Robot was commissioned by Shell-Mex in 1936 and combined an overt commercial message with experimental stop-motion. Humphrey Jennings also worked on it before becoming one of Britain's most important documentary filmmakers.

title: A fossil lizard relative is more than 241 million years old
body: Agriodontosaurus helsbypetrae, discovered in Devon, is the oldest known member of the group containing modern lizards, snakes and tuataras. It lived less than 10 million years after the end-Permian mass extinction.

title: A fossil reptile had a jaw twisted sideways on purpose
body: Tanyka amnicola lived 275 million years ago and had uniquely twisted jaws with sideways-facing teeth. Eight additional jaw fossils convinced researchers the strange geometry was anatomical, not damage.

title: A fossil shark spent 70 million years waiting to be named
body: A previously unknown shark species was identified from a fossil skeleton found in southern England, representing an animal that lived more than 70 million years ago. The skeleton survived; the name had to wait a little longer.

title: A fossil spent 60 years being the wrong animal
body: The material that became Sphenodraco had been misidentified for decades before researchers noticed that two apparently unrelated museum pieces fitted together. The resulting animal turns out to have been adapted to climbing.

title: A fungal partner may have helped plants survive Snowball Earth
body: Antarctic meltwater ponds currently support fungi, algae and other eukaryotes in conditions researchers think could resemble refuges available during Snowball Earth. Global temperatures during those ancient glaciations may have fallen below -50°C.

title: A fungus can digest plastic
body: Several fungi have been shown to degrade synthetic polymers under laboratory conditions, including polyurethane. The discovery does not mean discarded plastic will disappear in a forest, but fungal enzymes can attack materials once considered biologically inert.

title: A fungus can turn ants into walking corpses
body: Ophiocordyceps fungi infect ants and manipulate their behaviour before killing them in a location favourable for fungal reproduction. Different fungal species specialise in different ant hosts rather than infecting everything indiscriminately.

title: A fungus was already helping plants eat properly 400 million years ago
body: Fossils from the Rhynie Chert show fungi occupying plant tissues and apparently exchanging nutrients with their hosts. The partnership appears to have been established almost as soon as complex plants were colonising land.

title: A German church is currently 25 years into a 639-year-long organ performance
body: In 2001, a specialized mechanical organ in Halberstadt, Germany, began playing avant-garde composer John Cage's piece "As Slow As Possible." The incredibly slow, sustained performance is scheduled to conclude in the year 2640, with the most recent physical note change occurring on August 5, 2026.

title: A giant squid may have been 19 metres long
body: Fossils attributed to Nanaimoteuthis haggarti suggest a squid-like marine predator reaching about 19 metres in length. It lived in dinosaur-era seas and apparently occupied the top-predator niche.

title: A Glasgow film festival showed a movie made outside the normal filmmaking system
body: Welcome to G-Town, about shape-shifting aliens landing in Glasgow, was made outside traditional filmmaking pathways before getting a world premiere at Glasgow Film Festival. The festival explicitly presented its local-cinema setting as part of the point.

title: A Glasgow horror festival put a movie entirely inside one prison cell on its bill
body: FrightFest Glasgow 2026 opened with Jailbroken, an action thriller set entirely within a single prison cell. The Scottish production was co-produced by Up Helly Aa and starred David Hayman and Bryan Larkin.

title: A Glasgow shoot turned an entire city block into fake America
body: Marvel's 2025 Glasgow production of Spider-Man: Brand New Day installed fake construction sites, American flags and an invented production company identity in the city centre. The shoot was officially disguised under the code name “Blue Oasis.”

title: A glass frog can hide 89% of its red blood cells
body: When resting, the northern glass frog removes roughly 89% of its circulating red blood cells from view by packing them into its liver. Its translucent body becomes significantly harder for predators to detect.

title: A golden nurse shark was photographed for the first time
body: Fishermen in Costa Rica caught and released a six-foot nurse shark with bright golden skin and white eyes. Scientists attributed the appearance to an exceptionally rare combination of pigmentation conditions never previously documented in that species.

title: A grain of Ryugu contained a mineral never seen there before
body: Researchers examining material returned from asteroid Ryugu found djerfisherite, a mineral not previously seen in Ryugu-like meteorites. Its presence suggests the asteroid's supposedly primitive ingredients had a much stranger history than expected.

title: A Grand Canyon worm had a retractable throat
body: Kraytdraco spectatus was a 500-million-year-old priapulid worm with rows of internal spines and a throat it could extend and retract. Its body plan would look considerably stranger in a modern biology textbook than a typical earthworm.

title: A headless Raspberry Pi Zero consumes less than 0.5 watts of power
body: Without a graphical desktop environment running, the stripped-down Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W sips only about 0.4 to 0.7 watts at idle. A self-hoster could theoretically run the server 24/7 for an entire year and consume less electricity than a single 60-watt incandescent lightbulb uses in three days.

title: A horse can make two sounds at exactly the same time
body: Researchers found that a horse's whinny combines a low-frequency sound from the vocal folds with a higher-pitched whistle produced in the larynx. Humans can do something similar when beatboxing or throat-singing.

title: A jellyfish can reverse its own life cycle
body: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its mature medusa stage back into a juvenile polyp under severe stress. It is not literally immortal, but it can repeatedly restart its developmental sequence.

title: A Jurassic amphibian had a chameleon-style ballistic tongue
body: Nabia civiscientrix was only about five centimetres long, yet it could project its tongue at prey. Fossils from Portugal show that this specialised feeding mechanism existed roughly 150 million years ago.

title: A Jurassic parasite has been preserved for 165 million years
body: A Chinese fossil from the Jurassic period is the oldest known specimen of a thorny-headed worm, a parasite whose modern relatives anchor themselves inside a host's gut using rows of backward-facing hooks. Parasites, it turns out, had already perfected unpleasant engineering by then.

title: A living tree can be genetically older than its neighbours
body: Clonal trees can survive by repeatedly replacing individual trunks while remaining one genetic organism. Some colonies, including quaking aspens, are estimated to be tens of thousands of years old even though no single trunk is remotely that old.

title: A lizard specimen sat in a museum for 162 years
body: A Cuban anole collected in 1863 was only recently recognised as the second known specimen of its species. The discovery involved CT scanning the old specimen and resolving a mystery surrounding an animal scientists had barely seen.

title: A London mosquito is at least 1,000 years out of place
body: Genetic evidence suggests the London Underground mosquito's ancestors evolved in the Mediterranean more than a millennium ago. Its distinctive subterranean lifestyle therefore predates the railway it is now famous for.

title: A mammoth tooth preserved the oldest host-associated microbial DNA
body: The record-breaking DNA came from microbes living in or on mammoth bodies rather than from the mammoths themselves. Some of the organisms may have been involved in disease, giving scientists a glimpse of an ancient animal's microbiome.

title: A mantis shrimp punches with the acceleration of a .22 caliber bullet
body: The striking appendage of a peacock mantis shrimp moves so violently fast that it physically tears the water apart, creating a brief vacuum bubble. When this cavitation bubble collapses, it emits a flash of light and momentarily reaches temperatures nearing the surface of the sun.

title: A million seconds is 11 days, but a billion seconds is nearly 32 years
body: Human brains struggle to intuitively grasp the mathematical scale of large orders of magnitude. If you count backwards exactly one million seconds, you would land about a week and a half in the past, but counting backwards exactly one billion seconds throws you back 31.7 years into the 1990s.

title: A molecule in space has the chemistry of sugar
body: Erythrulose was detected in an interstellar cloud where stars and planets are forming. The discovery suggests some of the chemistry needed for life can arise before planets themselves exist.

title: A moth can fly hundreds of kilometres using the stars
body: Bogong moths emerge from their cocoons and travel long distances to the Australian Alps, where they spend the summer in caves. They have never visited those caves before but can still steer using the night sky.

title: A museum fossil split between two countries for 90 years became one reptile
body: Two fossil fragments held separately at London's Natural History Museum and Frankfurt's Senckenberg Museum were recognised as halves of the same animal. Reuniting them revealed a new Jurassic reptile that appears to have climbed trees.

title: A mythical Kryptonite mineral really exists, but it is white
body: Jadarite was discovered in Serbia in 2004 and has almost the same chemical composition as fictional Kryptonite. Unlike Superman's green mineral, the real substance is white and occurs in only one known valley.

title: A parasite can make rats less afraid of cats
body: Toxoplasma gondii infection has been linked to altered anti-predator behaviour in rodents, including reduced avoidance of cat odours. Cats are the parasite's definitive host, so the weirdness serves its reproductive interests.

title: A planet-sized moon was found around a brown dwarf
body: Astronomers reported a candidate exosatellite with roughly planetary mass orbiting a substellar companion rather than a normal star. If confirmed, it would be an extreme version of a moon: a world orbiting a failed star.

title: A plant can heat itself specifically to attract beetles
body: Some cycads warm their reproductive organs by several degrees and emit infrared radiation during the brief period when they need pollinators. The heat appears to act as a signal to specialised beetles moving through the dark.

title: A plant can literally glow in infrared to summon beetles
body: Male Zamia cycads heat their reproductive structures several hours before females, producing an infrared signal detectable by specialised beetles. The plants effectively advertise themselves with heat.

title: A pyramid in the Judean Desert may have been a tax office
body: A roughly 2,200-year-old pyramidal structure near the Dead Sea contained Greek papyri, coins, weapons, furniture and bronze vessels. Archaeologists think it may have begun as a Ptolemaic administrative station before later becoming a burial site.

title: A quantum experiment put 7,000 atoms into superposition
body: In January 2026, physicists reported creating a quantum superposition involving a system containing roughly 7,000 atoms. This pushed a famously microscopic phenomenon into a surprisingly large regime.

title: A rocky exoplanet may have an atmosphere made visible by escaping helium
body: Astronomers detected helium escaping from LHS 1140b, providing evidence that the rocky planet probably has an atmosphere. It orbits its star in the region where liquid water could theoretically exist.

title: A rogue star is currently fleeing the Milky Way at 3.9 million miles per hour
body: Astronomers tracking an ultra-fast main-sequence star known as S5-HVS1 calculated its trajectory directly back to the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy. The star was violently slingshotted out of the galactic core 5 million years ago and is currently rocketing into intergalactic space at a staggering 6 million kilometers per hour.

title: A Roman fort keeps producing enormous shoes
body: Archaeologists working at Magna, a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, have found unusually large leather shoes, including examples around modern US men's size 14. They still don't know why the inhabitants apparently had feet to match.

title: A Roman gladiator may have been dragged away by a lion
body: Bite marks on a human pelvis from a gladiator burial site in Britain are consistent with a large carnivore attack. Researchers say they provide the first physical evidence that gladiators in the Roman world actually fought lions.

title: A Roman person's brain turned into glass in seconds
body: A victim of the eruption of Vesuvius at Herculaneum had brain tissue vitrified by extreme heat. The glass-like material is evidence that the temperature around the person's head rose extraordinarily fast.

title: A Roman-era woman buried in Britain turned out to be British
body: DNA analysis of the “Beachy Head Woman” showed she was probably born in Britain, contradicting earlier suggestions of recent ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa or the Mediterranean. Her skeleton had been discovered in a box in a town-hall basement in 2012.

title: A Scottish archaeologist found a stone circle because visitors were wearing out the peat
body: Historic Environment Scotland's geophysicists surveyed an informal walking route at Machrie Moor partly because visitors were creating erosion tracks. Beneath the peat they found Machrie 12, a 28-by-25-metre prehistoric circle apparently the site's largest.

title: A Scottish archive stores 23,491 moving-image catalogue records as downloadable data
body: The National Library of Scotland publishes its Moving Image Archive metadata as a dataset containing 23,491 catalogue records. A national film archive can therefore be queried like a database rather than merely browsed like a catalogue.

title: A Scottish archive uncovered Vietnamese refugee footage made by amateurs
body: The National Library's home-movie collection contains amateur footage of Vietnamese boat refugees arriving in Scotland in the early 1980s. The footage was made by ordinary people rather than news crews and was later rediscovered by researchers.

title: A Scottish council consultation attracted exactly eight responses
body: Aberdeenshire Council's 2025 development-plan consultation received only eight responses despite substantial online traffic. One respondent objected to the use of planning “quarters” because months or seasons would be easier to understand.

title: A Scottish director rehearsed his actors for a month before filming Harvest
body: Athina Rachel Tsangari assembled the large cast in Oban for about a month, where they rehearsed, danced and walked the land together. She rewrote the script every evening and arrived on set with a fixed shooting script rather than improvising.

title: A Scottish film about fake Californian rappers was actually based on a real scam
body: Dundee duo Silibil N' Brains invented American identities because they believed their Scottish accents were blocking their music career. They managed to convince people in the US music industry that the fictional Californian rappers were real.

title: A Scottish film crew spent six weeks climbing through peat bogs carrying equipment
body: During the Scottish shoot for The Eagle, there was no road to one remote location. Crew members walked roughly 20 minutes each way through boggy ground in the dark, while the desired bad weather helpfully arrived every day for six weeks.

title: A Scottish film production fund put £400,000 behind a Lockerbie drama
body: Screen Scotland's Production Growth Fund contributed £400,000 to Lockerbie: A Search for Truth. The series then recreated parts of the story using Linlithgow as one of its Scottish locations.

title: A Scottish fossil plant was only a few centimetres tall
body: A 400-million-year-old Rhynie plant, Horneophyton lignieri, was only a few centimetres high but contained cells resembling precursors of modern xylem and phloem. The vascular architecture that eventually helped plants reach 100 metres began with something closer to table decor.

title: A Scottish golf-course dig uncovered a 2,000-year-old chariot tyre
body: Archaeologists near Inverness initially mistook a large iron object for old agricultural equipment. It proved to be the metal tyre of an Iron Age chariot, an unusually rare find in Scotland.

title: A Scottish library lends boxes containing artificial sunlight
body: East Dunbartonshire libraries lend “Wintering Well Boxes” containing equipment and activities intended to help people through the darker months. The scheme began as a local pilot and expanded to Orkney in 2025.

title: A Scottish library put teenagers in charge of the mobile branch
body: One Scottish mobile-library model turns its vehicle into a youth centre after the daytime library route ends, swapping shelves for desks, laptops, Wi-Fi and a kitchen. The same bus effectively has a second job after closing time.

title: A Scottish oak has survived roughly 500 years
body: The Birnam Oak is described by the University of Birmingham as the oldest surviving tree of the historic Birnam Wood associated with Macbeth. In 2025, researchers successfully cultivated six saplings from its acorns.

title: A Scottish shipwreck was dated by tree rings to trees felled in 1748–1762
body: A winter storm exposed a wreck on Sanday in Orkney; dendrochronologists sampled the oak and narrowed the ship's timber to 1748–1762. That let researchers identify it as HMS Hind, later renamed the Earl of Chatham and turned into a whaler.

title: A sea spider can keep its organs inside its legs
body: More than 1,300 sea-spider species are known, and their strange anatomy lets organs extend deep into their limbs. Some species effectively carry their digestive machinery through their walking legs.

title: A seal tooth pendant sat unidentified for almost 160 years
body: A mysterious object excavated in Devon in the Victorian era has finally been identified as a pendant made from the tooth of a male grey seal. Wear marks show that someone actually suspended it from a cord more than 15,000 years ago.

title: A shark fossil spent decades disguised as something else
body: Pararhincodon torquis was identified from fossil material in British chalk that had not previously been recognised as belonging to this distant relative of modern carpet sharks. The animal lived around 85 million years ago.

title: A shark turned gold without becoming albino
body: A nurse shark filmed in Costa Rica had striking golden-yellow skin and pale eyes. Scientists attributed the unusual appearance to a rare pigmentation condition rather than conventional albinism.

title: A simple software bug vaporized a $370 million European rocket
body: During its maiden flight in 1996, the Ariane 5 rocket violently exploded just 37 seconds after liftoff. The catastrophic failure was triggered when a legacy piece of code attempted to stuff a 64-bit floating-point number into a 16-bit signed integer space, instantly crashing the primary and backup guidance computers.

title: A single 4.5:1 number decides whether ordinary text passes WCAG AA
body: WCAG's normal-text contrast requirement uses a minimum ratio of 4.5:1 for AA conformance; large text can use 3:1. A visually plausible grey can therefore be objectively non-compliant by a decimal-sized margin.

title: A single battered moth helped reveal 11 species
body: A 1.2-centimetre museum moth collected by Alfred Russel Wallace in 1855 turned out to belong to a genus containing 14 species, 11 of them new to science. DNA sequencing extracted from a tiny fragment of leg solved what morphology had not.

title: A single block of 256 IPv4 addresses now costs roughly $13,000
body: Because the global pool of 4.3 billion standard IPv4 internet addresses completely ran out in 2011, a massive secondary auction market has emerged. Network operators now routinely pay around $50 per individual IP address just to keep legacy routing systems functional while the world slowly transitions to IPv6.

title: A single day on Venus mathematically outlasts an entire Venusian year
body: Because Venus rotates on its axis at a sluggish, retrograde crawl, it takes the equivalent of 243 Earth days to complete just one physical spin. However, its proximity to the Sun means it completes a full solar orbit in only 225 Earth days, making a local year physically shorter than a local day.

title: A single expedition found a siphonophore that may be an entirely new genus
body: Researchers used laser-based imaging to scan delicate midwater animals without touching them. One siphonophore photographed at roughly 350–552 metres may represent a genus not previously known to science.

title: A single fossil specimen sat unnoticed through 150 years of collecting
body: The coelacanth fossil eventually named Macropoma gombessae had been in London's Natural History Museum collections for generations before researchers recognised its importance. Museum drawers can still contain evolutionary “missing links”.

title: A single human body contains 60,000 miles of blood vessels
body: The human circulatory system relies on a microscopic, highly branched network of capillaries to deliver oxygen to every single cell. If you were to extract and lay out all the arteries, veins, and capillaries from an average adult end-to-end, they would stretch roughly 60,000 miles—long enough to wrap around the Earth's equator almost two and a half times.

title: A single museum study turned five species into 16
body: The butterfly revision was based partly on museum specimens rather than fresh field discoveries. Old drawers therefore contained nine species that science had not previously recognised as separate.

title: A single prehistoric city left 5,000 holes in a mountainside
body: Monte Sierpe in Peru contains roughly 5,000 holes arranged across a mountainside. Drone mapping suggests the pits may have held baskets of goods and formed part of an accounting or marketplace system.

title: A single prehistoric frog fossil preserved a final meal
body: Scientists studying exceptionally preserved fossil frogs found evidence of prey still inside the digestive tract. The fossil captures not merely what the animal looked like, but what it was eating shortly before death.

title: A single Roman skeleton may finally prove the arena stories
body: Ancient writers described gladiators fighting lions, but archaeological evidence had been elusive. A male skeleton from York with carnivore bite marks may be the physical confirmation that this particular kind of spectacle really occurred.

title: A single teaspoon of a neutron star weighs as much as 900 Great Pyramids
body: When a massive star collapses, its core compresses into a sphere so dense that protons and electrons melt into pure neutrons. The resulting material is so tightly packed that one cubic centimeter—roughly the size of a sugar cube—weighs 1 billion tons.

title: A single, coordinated ant colony spans three different continents
body: The Argentine ant is biologically wired to recognize and cooperate with its own genetic relatives. Because humans inadvertently transported identical lineages across the globe, an aggressive "mega-colony" of perfectly cooperative ants now spans thousands of miles across California, Europe, and Japan, forming the largest known insect society on Earth.

title: A snail can sleep for years
body: Some land snails can enter prolonged dormancy during dry periods, slowing their metabolism dramatically and remaining inactive for months or even years. “Sleeping through the bad weather” is therefore a legitimate gastropod survival strategy.

title: A solar system was caught just as planets started forming
body: Astronomers observed HOPS-315, a very young star surrounded by material showing the earliest stages of planet formation. It is effectively a newborn version of the Solar System captured during the dusty, chaotic bit.

title: A sourdough jar can change the aroma without changing the bread's nutrition
body: A 2025 study compared four traditional sourdough propagation methods and found that water-propagated starters produced a more complex aromatic profile. Yet protein digestibility and glycaemic characteristics of the resulting breads were hardly affected by the propagation method.

title: A space telescope found sugar molecules in another solar system's nursery
body: Astronomers detected erythrulose, a four-carbon sugar, in gas and dust near the centre of the Milky Way. It is the most complex true sugar yet detected outside our Solar System.

title: A spider-like brain is 500 million years old
body: Fossils of Mollisonia preserve a nervous system with a protocerebrum-like region containing pathways associated with vision. It may be the earliest evidence of a brain structure recognisably on the arthropod side of the family tree.

title: A Spinosaurus had a sword-shaped crest on its head
body: Spinosaurus mirabilis had a large blade-like crest rising from its skull. The new species lived about 95 million years ago in what is now the Sahara, when the region was wetland rather than desert.

title: A stuffed hedgehog was caught 60 nautical miles offshore
body: During a 2025 NOAA survey in the Gulf of Maine, scientists hauling a one-mile-long line with 1,000 hooks unexpectedly recovered a muddy stuffed hedgehog covered in filter-feeding organisms. It was about as biologically unhelpful as a specimen can get.

title: A T-Rex lived closer in time to the iPad than to the Stegosaurus
body: The Stegosaurus went extinct roughly 150 million years ago, while the Tyrannosaurus Rex didn't evolve until about 67 million years ago. This massive 83-million-year gap means less time separates a T-Rex from modern humanity than separates the two famous dinosaurs.

title: A tardigrade can survive boiling water but not being roasted
body: Tardigrades are famous for surviving extreme conditions, but heat tolerance depends strongly on their hydrated or desiccated state and on exposure time. They are not universally indestructible, despite the internet having promoted them as microscopic tanks.

title: A teaspoon of neutron-star matter weighs about a billion tons
body: NASA gives the familiar scale of neutron-star density as roughly a billion tons for one teaspoon of material on Earth. One teaspoon, in this case, is doing an astonishing amount of rhetorical work. I logged this on 2025-11-26.

title: A teaspoon of water holds more molecules than the Atlantic holds teaspoons
body: The sheer mathematical scale of molecular physics defies human intuition. There are roughly $1.67 \times 10^{23}$ individual water molecules physically packed into a single teaspoon, which is approximately three times greater than the total number of physical teaspoons of water contained in the entire Atlantic Ocean.

title: A telecom cable became 44,000 earthquake sensors
body: Researchers turned a 4,400-kilometre fibre-optic cable between California and Hawaii into the equivalent of 44,000 seismic detectors. Stretching the glass changes how light travels through it.

title: A tiny Cambrian predator was named after Mothra
body: Mosura fentoni was a finger-sized predator that lived more than 500 million years ago and had a body plan incorporating features that later evolved separately in crustaceans and arachnids. Its researchers named it after the giant Japanese monster Mothra.

title: A tiny Jurassic amphibian had a projectile tongue
body: Nabia civiscientrix was only a few centimetres long but apparently launched its tongue to seize prey. Fossil bones show this chameleon-like trick existed roughly 150 million years ago.

title: A tree falling in the Amazon exposed human burial urns
body: When a large tree toppled in Brazil, its roots pulled two enormous ceramic vessels out of the ground. Archaeologists identified them as funerary urns belonging to an Indigenous culture whose pottery tradition is not yet understood.

title: A tree falling in the Amazon exposed human burials
body: A toppled tree uprooted ceramic funerary vessels from beneath the soil in the Brazilian Amazon. The accident exposed archaeology that would otherwise have remained invisible under living forest.

title: A tree rat has opposable thumbs and a prehensile tail
body: Emmons's tree rat, known from only a tiny number of observations, has opposable thumb-like digits and a tail capable of gripping branches. A DNA study has now confirmed its distinct evolutionary identity.

title: A tsunami may have become a geological time capsule full of tree resin
body: Amber normally begins as sticky tree resin that later fossilises. A Japanese deposit appears to have been rapidly buried and moved by marine disturbance, preserving evidence of both ancient forests and powerful waves.

title: A tumour can become an infectious disease
body: The transmissible catfish cancer discovered in 2026 joins only a tiny list of known naturally contagious cancers. In these cases, living tumour cells themselves pass between animals and establish a new tumour.

title: A typical garden snail's mouth is mathematically packed with 14,000 teeth
body: Snails do not chew their food; they aggressively scrape it away using a ribbon-like structure called a radula. This microscopic biological chainsaw is lined with thousands of microscopic, chitinous teeth, and as the front rows mathematically wear down from grinding against rocks and leaves, new teeth continually grow in the back to replace them.

title: A utility worker found a thousand-year-old mummy four feet underground
body: Gas workers installing pipes in Lima discovered a seated child mummy about four feet below the modern street. The child, probably aged 10–15, had retained visible dark-brown hair after roughly a millennium underground.

title: A velvet worm was found in a place velvet worms supposedly hate
body: A new velvet worm species was discovered in the semi-arid Little Karoo of South Africa, despite its relatives normally living in humid forest. Genetic evidence suggests the population split from its relatives about 15.2 million years ago.

title: A vulture nest preserved a 750-year-old shoe
body: A grass-and-twig sandal found in a bearded-vulture nest in southern Spain is roughly 727–771 years old. The dry cave environment and continual reuse of the nest stopped something ordinarily biodegradable from disappearing.

title: A weedkiller could be linked to 1.4 million AMR deaths indirectly
body: Antimicrobial resistance is associated with an estimated 1.1–1.4 million deaths each year, according to the WHO figures cited by researchers studying glyphosate's possible role. The interesting part is that the environmental route may connect an agricultural chemical to a hospital problem.

title: A Welsh physics teacher now has a 215-million-year-old crocodile named after him
body: Galahadosuchus jonesi was identified from a fossil discovered in southwest England in 1969 and only recognised as a new species decades later. Its namesake is a secondary-school physics teacher who inspired one of the researchers.

title: A West Virginia town legally banned Wi-Fi to protect a telescope
body: The town of Green Bank sits within the US National Radio Quiet Zone, an area enforcing severe legal restrictions on electromagnetic radiation. To prevent interference with the hyper-sensitive Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope, the local government strictly bans Wi-Fi routers, cell towers, and even microwave ovens, mathematically preserving a pristine zone of radio silence.

title: A whale graveyard was found 7 kilometres beneath the ocean
body: A deep-sea submersible discovered a concentration of whale bones and other fossils in the Diamantina Fracture Zone. One fossil represented a previously unknown species of extinct beaked whale.

title: A whale necropolis stretches 1,200 kilometres across the seafloor
body: A deep-sea expedition found five modern whale-fall communities and 476 fossil cetaceans spread across roughly 1,200 kilometres of the Diamantina Fracture Zone. Some remains are at depths approaching 7,000 metres.

title: A wobbling asteroid once had liquid water
body: NASA's Lucy spacecraft found that the peanut-shaped asteroid Donaldjohanson was created by a violent collision about 155 million years ago and retains evidence of a brief episode involving liquid water. An asteroid can therefore have both a plumbing history and a collision history.

title: A wood frog can freeze solid and thaw back to life
body: Wood frogs survive winter with as much as two-thirds of the water in their bodies frozen. Their blood and tissues are protected by glucose and other cryoprotective chemistry.

title: A woodpecker's tongue wraps completely around its brain for protection
body: Woodpeckers sustain zero brain damage despite violently slamming their beaks into solid wood at 15 miles per hour up to 12,000 times a day. They survive this trauma because their exceptionally long, muscular tongue splits at the base of the throat, physically wraps around the back of the skull, and anchors in the right nostril to act as a biological shock absorber.

title: A £50 monthly travel allowance helped half of poor households get or keep jobs
body: Solent Mobility Credits gives low-income participants £50 a month to spend on buses, ferries and other local transport. Early monitoring found 97% of surveyed participants said it improved wellbeing, while more than half said it helped them find or stay in a job.

title: A “lost” echidna resurfaced after 62 years
body: Attenborough's long-beaked echidna had no scientific evidence of its survival since 1961. Camera traps finally photographed it in 2023, confirming that one of the world's most mysterious lost mammals was still alive.

title: A “mystery dinosaur” was hiding in one of the world's best-studied fossil beds
body: Enigmacursor mollyborthwickae was identified from a small fossil from Colorado's Morrison Formation, a deposit that has been worked for well over a century. It shows that even famous dinosaur quarries can contain overlooked species.

title: Aardman shot a 101-metre Wallace & Gromit film on an iPhone
body: Aardman captured an entire stop-motion advert on iPhone 16 Pro Max cameras, delivering a final image large enough to cover the 101-metre Battersea Power Station towers. The main sequence ran for more than 600 frames with hidden cuts.

title: Aardman's Disastrous 2005 Archive Fire
body: In 2005, a devastating warehouse fire completely destroyed the entire thirty-year physical history of Aardman Animations in Bristol. Every single claymation puppet, miniature set, and prop used in the original Wallace and Gromit shorts and Chicken Run was melted into slag, wiping out a cornerstone of British cinematic history in a single night.

title: Aberdeenshire built a free matchmaking service for empty houses
body: Its Matchmaker scheme lets owners of empty properties list them for free while the council introduces potential buyers and points owners toward renovation grants, discounts and council-tax incentives. It is essentially a dating service for houses nobody can sell.

title: Acid house was accidentally invented on a failed guitar practice tool
body: Roland released the TB-303 bass synthesizer in 1981 intending it to replace human bassists for solo guitarists practicing at home. It sounded nothing like a real bass guitar and was a total commercial flop, until Chicago electronic producers bought them from pawn shops, pushed the filter knobs to extreme resonance, and created the squelching sound of acid house.

title: Adding sourdough did not change how quickly wholemeal bread digested in vitro
body: Researchers compared wholemeal breads made with different sourdough starters and fermentation regimes. In their laboratory digestion model, adding sourdough did not change the kinetics of starch digestion.

title: AI designed a CRISPR protein that edited human DNA
body: OpenCRISPR-1 was generated by an AI model rather than discovered in nature. Experiments showed it could edit human DNA while substantially reducing some off-target effects compared with conventional CRISPR systems.

title: Alaska is simultaneously the northernmost, westernmost, and easternmost US state
body: Geographically, Alaska obviously holds the records for being the furthest north and west. However, because the remote volcanic islands of the Aleutian chain physically stretch across the 180th meridian line, the state officially crosses over into the Eastern Hemisphere, making it the easternmost state as well.

title: Alaskan wood frogs survive the winter by freezing 65% of their body solid
body: When temperatures drop below freezing, the Alaskan wood frog completely stops its heart, ceases all breathing, and allows its brain activity to flatline. It floods its bloodstream with glucose acting as a biological antifreeze, allowing up to 65% of the total water in its body to turn to solid ice for months until it magically thaws and hops away in the spring.

title: Alien 3's Rejected Wooden Planet
body: The original script for Alien 3 took place entirely on an artificial, technologically advanced wooden planet populated by Luddite monks. Fox executives spent millions building massive timber sets at Pinewood Studios before panicking, firing director Vincent Ward, and awkwardly forcing the new crew to retrofit the existing wooden scaffolding into a bleak, concrete prison colony.

title: Alien's Borrowed Rock Band Laser
body: For the scene in Alien (1979) where the crew investigates the massive space jockey egg chamber, Ridley Scott couldn't afford complex optical effects for a protective blue force field. He simply borrowed a massive laser system from the British rock band The Who, who happened to be testing their stage lighting rig in the exact next-door soundstage at Shepperton Studios.

title: Alien's Soho Pub Monster
body: To make the Xenomorph look inhumanly proportioned and physically wrong in Ridley Scott's 1979 film Alien, casting agents scoured London for exceptionally thin, tall non-actors. They eventually found Bolaji Badejo, a 6'10" Nigerian graphic design student, having a drink in a Soho pub and immediately put him in the suit.

title: Amazon researchers found 432 ancient geometric earthworks
body: Aerial imaging uncovered 432 previously unrecorded geoglyph-like structures in southwestern Amazonia. Researchers estimate the wider region may contain 24,000–30,000 such earthworks.

title: An Aberdeenshire tree-planting scheme gives farmers the trees, stakes and labour plan for free
body: The Sma Wids scheme asks participating landowners mainly to do the planting and maintenance, while the project supplies trees and materials and provides one-to-one design help. The pilot planted more than 4,000 trees across just ten tiny woods.

title: An Acupuncture Needle Solves Espresso Channeling
body: In 2005, computer science professor John Weiss created the Weiss Distribution Technique (WDT) to eliminate clumps in finely ground espresso that cause uneven extraction. His original, highly effective tool was simply a series of 0.4mm acupuncture needles jammed into a wine cork.

title: An ancient fossil had to be identified nine times before anyone believed it
body: Researchers initially wondered whether the nine twisted jaws of Tanyka were damaged or belonged to fish. Only after finding repeated examples could they establish that the bizarre morphology belonged to one previously unknown species.

title: An ancient reptile's jaws turned sideways
body: Tanyka amnicola had uniquely twisted jaws carrying sideways-facing teeth, apparently adapted for grinding food. Nine separate fossils proved the strange shape was real anatomy rather than damage.

title: An ancient “octopus” turned out to be a nautilus relative
body: The 310-million-year-old fossil Pohlsepia mazonensis was long celebrated as the oldest known octopus. A 2026 study concluded it is actually related to Nautilus, removing a supposed 150-million-year jump in octopus history.

title: An ancient “turtle ancestor” turned out to be a burrowing reptile
body: Eunotosaurus was long considered a primitive member of the turtle lineage because of its broad ribs. New CT scans instead place it among millerettids, suggesting its turtle-like ribcage evolved independently.

title: An ankylosaur had its tail weapon 30 million years too early
body: Spicomellus is the oldest known ankylosaur and appears to have had a tail weapon more than 30 million years before similar structures became common in later ankylosaurs. Its armour makes several standard ideas about ankylosaur evolution awkward.

title: An Apollo 17 core sat sealed for more than 50 years
body: A lunar core collected in 1972 was finally opened with modern scanning technology in 2025. Its contents helped explain a five-kilometre-long deposit on the Moon as the remains of an ancient landslide.

title: An Arctic mountain contains 30,000 fossils from an ecosystem three million years after extinction
body: A bonebed on Spitsbergen contains more than 30,000 marine fossils dating to about 249 million years ago. The diversity suggests local seas rebounded from the end-Permian catastrophe much faster than the global picture implies.

title: An Arctic mountain contains more than 30,000 marine fossils
body: Researchers found a 249-million-year-old marine bonebed halfway up Mount Marmier on Spitsbergen, containing more than 30,000 fossils. The site captures an ocean ecosystem that now happens to be several hundred metres above sea level.

title: An asteroid once had a 4.3% chance of hitting the Moon
body: Before new James Webb observations, asteroid 2024 YR4 had an estimated 4.3% probability of striking the Moon on 22 December 2032. New observations reduced that possibility to zero and put its predicted miss distance at about 21,200 kilometres.

title: An average, fluffy white cumulus cloud weighs over 1 million pounds
body: Despite floating gracefully in the sky, clouds possess immense physical mass due to their sheer volume of condensed water droplets. A typical cumulus cloud—measuring about one cubic kilometer in size—holds roughly 500,000 kilograms of liquid water, equivalent to the weight of 100 elephants suspended in the air.

title: An Egyptian man's 4,500-year-old genome was 80% North African
body: The oldest and most complete ancient Egyptian genome yet sequenced came from a man buried at Nuwyat. About 80% of his ancestry was linked to Neolithic North Africa and 20% to populations associated with West Asia.

title: An Indonesian QR code system now serves 41 million merchants
body: Indonesia's national QRIS system had about 41 million merchants by late 2025, more than 90% of them micro, small or medium businesses. QRIS processed roughly 2.5 billion transactions during 2025.

title: An interstellar comet was already active months before discovery
body: 3I/ATLAS appears to have been releasing gas and dust for months before astronomers formally recognised it. A passing object from another planetary system had therefore been quietly visible in hindsight.

title: An “octopus” fossil was actually related to Nautilus
body: Pohlsepia, a 310-million-year-old fossil long treated as the oldest octopus, has been reclassified as a nautilus relative. The change removes a supposed 150-million-year gap from the octopus fossil record.

title: Ancient animal tracks preserve 20 million years of sensory evolution
body: Researchers used fossilised tracks to investigate how early animals changed from seemingly aimless movement to purposeful journeys over roughly 20 million years. Bodies rarely fossilise this well; the footprints sometimes do the talking.

title: Ancient Australians may have had amniote ancestors 356 million years ago
body: Fossil footprints in Australia have been dated to 356 million years ago, potentially putting the ancestors of reptiles, birds and mammals about 40 million years earlier than expected. The oldest known tracks are doing more damage to the textbook than a skeleton would.

title: Ancient poison arrows may be 60,000 years old
body: Chemical residues on prehistoric arrowheads from Africa indicate that humans were deliberately applying toxic substances to hunting weapons around 60,000 years ago. The technology implies planning, experimentation and an unexpectedly sophisticated knowledge of local poisons.

title: Ancient Saharan DNA suggests farming spread without mass migration
body: Genomes from people living in the “Green Sahara” about 7,000 years ago suggest pastoralism spread largely through cultural transmission rather than wholesale replacement by migrants. The technology moved faster than the genes.

title: Ancient Salvadoran dolls had detachable heads
body: Five ceramic figurines dating to roughly 410–380 BCE had moveable heads and expressive open mouths. They may have been manipulated like puppets, making them remarkably early examples of articulated toys or ritual figures.

title: Andean hunters built walls 150 metres long to funnel vicuñas
body: Ancient communities in what is now Chile constructed huge V-shaped stone hunting traps, some around 150 metres long. The walls funnelled wild vicuñas toward enclosures where hunters could capture them in groups.

title: Animators hand-drew 82,080 frames of lighting for Who Framed Roger Rabbit
body: To seamlessly blend 2D ink-and-paint characters with live-action 1947 Hollywood, Disney animators painstakingly generated 82,080 individual frames of animation. They then re-shot every single cel through multiple layers of optical contrast masks to generate realistic, moving shadows that perfectly matched the live-action on-set lighting.

title: Antarctica's Blood Falls is effectively ancient rust leaking from a glacier
body: The famous red waterfall contains salty brine rich in iron, which oxidises when it meets oxygen. New work supports the idea that the water originates from ancient seawater trapped beneath the ice millions of years ago.

title: Antarctica's first known dinosaur fossil was a titanosaur
body: A vertebra collected in Antarctica has been identified as the continent's first confirmed dinosaur fossil. The animal was a titanosaur, a group of long-necked herbivores that included some of the largest land animals ever.

title: Aphex Twin mathematically embedded a photograph of his grinning face into a track
body: Near the end of the 1999 track "Equation" (also known as "Formula"), Richard D. James programmed specific high-frequency audio data that sounds like abrasive noise to the naked ear. When that audio is processed through a spectrogram, it visually renders a terrifying, high-contrast photograph of James' own face.

title: Aphex Twin's Armored Commute
body: Electronic musician Richard D. James (Aphex Twin) famously purchased a fully functioning 1950s Ferret Mark 1 armoured scout car. He outfitted the interior with a sound system and drove the military vehicle around the narrow country lanes of Cornwall as his personal transport.

title: Aphex Twin's Sandpaper DJ Set
body: Playing a gig at London's experimental Disobey club in the mid-1990s, Richard D. James (Aphex Twin) became bored of standard DJing conventions. He spent his set violently throwing sheets of industrial sandpaper onto the spinning turntables and running a kitchen food mixer through a chain of guitar delay pedals.

title: Apple's 2007 iPhone calculator was a direct copy of a 1987 Dieter Rams design
body: The layout, rounded buttons, and precise color-coding of mathematical operations on the original iOS calculator were lifted almost verbatim from the Braun ET 66 pocket calculator. The visual grammar of organizing operations by color without needing text labels was pioneered by Dieter Rams and Dietrich Lubs.

title: Apple's Dimension-for-Dimension Homage to Braun
body: Apple's original 2001 iPod design was heavily inspired by the 1958 Braun T3 pocket radio designed by Dieter Rams, matching its proportions and scrolling wheel interface almost exactly. Rams publicly stated he viewed the design as a sincere compliment rather than corporate theft.

title: Apple's mobile UI caused a 15-year layout bug that required a new CSS unit
body: Because Mobile Safari dynamically collapses its address bar on scroll, setting a web layout to `100vh` traditionally caused the bottom of elements to bleed off-screen. It took over a decade for the W3C to introduce the `dvh` (dynamic viewport height) unit specifically to account for physical browser UI shifts.

title: Archimedes Lifts a 600-Tonne Boat
body: The Falkirk Wheel in Scotland is a massive, rotating boat lift that raises vessels 24 meters into the air.
